summary.text: Assume either family is bounded by \(N\), and apply the hypothesis to \(n=(N+2)!\) to obtain \(x+y=n\), with \(p=6x-1\) Sophie Germain and \(6y-1,6y+1\) twin primes. If the Sophie Germain primes are bounded, then \(p\mid n\) and hence \(p\mid(6y+1)\); if the twin pairs are bounded, then \(6y+1\le N+2\), so \(6y+1\mid n\) and hence \(6y+1\mid p\); in either case primality forces equality, impossible because the two numbers are respectively \(-1\) and \(1\pmod 6\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ is prime and }2p+1\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of Sophie Germain primes, and let
\[
T=\{r\in\mathbb N:r\text{ is prime and }r+2\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of lower members of twin-prime pairs.

For a positive integer \(n\), the number \(a(n)=A227923(n)\) is obtained by considering every integer \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\), putting \(y=n-x\), and counting \(x\) precisely when all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6y-1,\qquad 6y+1
\]
are prime. Notice that
\[
12x-1=2(6x-1)+1,
\]
so the first two primality conditions say that \(6x-1\) is a Sophie Germain prime, while the last two say that \(6y-1\) and \(6y+1\) form a twin-prime pair.

Assume the conjectural positivity statement
\[
 a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every integer }n>1. \tag{H}
\]
We prove that both \(S\) and \(T\) are infinite.

First record the immediate consequence of positivity that will be used twice. If \(a(n)>0\), then at least one summand in the defining finite sum for \(a(n)\) is nonzero. Every summand is either zero or one, so for some \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\), the corresponding primality condition holds. Set \(y=n-x\). Since \(x<n\), we have \(y\ge1\), and
\[
x+y=n.
\]
Thus there are positive integers \(x,y\) such that
\[
x+y=n \tag{1}
\]
and
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1 \tag{2}
\]
are all prime.

We shall also use two elementary facts. First, if \(1\le d\le m\), then \(d\mid m!\), because \(d\) is one of the factors occurring in \(m!\). Second, every positive divisor of a prime number is either \(1\) or the prime itself.

### Infinitely many Sophie Germain primes

It is enough to prove that \(S\) is not bounded above, since every finite set of natural numbers has an upper bound. Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(S\) is bounded above. Choose \(N\in\mathbb N\) such that
\[
p\le N\qquad\text{for every }p\in S. \tag{3}
\]

Take
\[
n=(N+2)!.
\]
Because \(N+2\ge2\), we have \(n\ge2\), and in particular \(n>1\). Hypothesis (H), together with the witness consequence established above, supplies positive integers \(x,y\) satisfying (1) and (2) for this value of \(n\).

Put
\[
p=6x-1,\qquad q=6y+1.
\]
The number \(p\) is prime by (2), and
\[
2p+1=2(6x-1)+1=12x-1
\]
is also prime. Hence \(p\in S\), and therefore the assumed bound (3) gives
\[
p\le N.
\]
Since \(p\) is prime it is positive, so \(1\le p\le N+2\). Consequently
\[
p\mid (N+2)!=n,
\]
and hence \(p\mid 6n\).

On the other hand, using \(x+y=n\), we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
p+q
  &=(6x-1)+(6y+1)\\
  &=6(x+y)\\
  &=6n.
\end{aligned} \tag{4}
\]
Thus \(p\mid p+q\). Since of course \(p\mid p\), subtraction in (4) shows that
\[
p\mid q. \tag{5}
\]
The number \(q=6y+1\) is prime by (2). Therefore (5) implies that either \(p=1\) or \(p=q\). The first alternative is impossible because \(p\) is prime (indeed, \(x\ge1\) even gives \(p\ge5\)). The second alternative is also impossible: it would say
\[
6x-1=6y+1,
\]
but the left side is congruent to \(5\pmod 6\), whereas the right side is congruent to \(1\pmod 6\). Equivalently, it would force a multiple of \(6\) to equal \(2\).

This contradiction shows that no upper bound \(N\) for \(S\) exists. Hence \(S\), the set of Sophie Germain primes, is infinite.

### Infinitely many twin-prime pairs

Again it suffices to show that \(T\) is unbounded. Suppose instead that there is an \(N\in\mathbb N\) such that
\[
r\le N\qquad\text{for every }r\in T. \tag{6}
\]

As before, let
\[
n=(N+2)!>1.
\]
By (H), choose positive integers \(x,y\) with \(x+y=n\) for which all four numbers in (2) are prime. Define
\[
r=6y-1,
\qquad q=6y+1,
\qquad p=6x-1.
\]
Since both \(r\) and
\[
r+2=(6y-1)+2=6y+1=q
\]
are prime, \(r\in T\). The assumed bound (6) therefore gives \(r\le N\). It follows that
\[
q=r+2\le N+2.
\]
Also \(q\) is prime and hence positive. Thus \(1\le q\le N+2\), so the factorial divisibility fact gives
\[
q\mid (N+2)!=n,
\]
and consequently \(q\mid6n\).

The same sum identity as before gives
\[
p+q=(6x-1)+(6y+1)=6(x+y)=6n. \tag{7}
\]
Hence \(q\mid p+q\). Since \(q\mid q\), subtracting \(q\) from (7) yields
\[
q\mid p. \tag{8}
\]
But \(p=6x-1\) is prime. Therefore its positive divisor \(q\) must be either \(1\) or \(p\). The possibility \(q=1\) is impossible, since \(y\ge1\) gives \(q=6y+1\ge7\). The possibility \(q=p\) is likewise impossible modulo \(6\): \(q=6y+1\) is congruent to \(1\pmod6\), while \(p=6x-1\) is congruent to \(5\pmod6\).

This contradiction proves that \(T\) has no upper bound and is therefore infinite. Since each element \(r\in T\) represents the twin-prime pair \((r,r+2)\), there are infinitely many twin-prime pairs.

We have proved from (H) that there are both infinitely many Sophie Germain primes and infinitely many twin-prime pairs, as claimed.
